newsitem.title: USA: CPI bias doesn't signal stable prices -- Fed experts.
newsitem.headline: CPI bias doesn't signal stable prices -- Fed experts.

text.p: - The growing consensus that the U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) overstates the level of inflation does not indicate the Federal Reserve is any closer to achieving its goal of price stability, Fed officials told Reuters in a series of interviews.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan and other top Fed officials have argued for quite some time that CPI overstates the true level of U.S. inflation. Yet no Fed official believes current CPI growth indicates price stability, said Charles Steindel, vice president for research at the New York Fed.
"This does not change our view of the world," Steindel said. "The goal of Fed policy remains long-term price stability. We are not at price stability."
A commission of academics, led by Stanford University professor Michael Boskin, on Wednesday reported to Congress that CPI overstates inflation by 1.1 percentage point.
CPI rose 3.0 percent through the 12 months ending in October and the core rate, excluding food and energy, of 2.6 percent.

Michael Bryan, Cleveland Fed assistant vice president for research and an expert on the CPI, said it is hard to estimate the extent of CPI bias. One of the easier aspects to measure is a relatively small substitution bias -- the ability of consumers to find cheaper alternatives when prices rise for a good or service.

But he said it is more difficult to measure so-called quality biases, such as new car models that are moderately more expensive than older models yet may also be substantially longer-lasting and cheaper to maintain.
Still, Bryan noted that CPI inflation, even after adjustments for bias, does not indicate the U.S. economy has stable prices.
"I don't think anybody believes the bias is large enough to conclude we have already arrived at price stability," Bryan said. "Saying the bias is large is premature and speculative."
"As the rate of infation goes down, the debate about how large is this mismeasurement is going to become a bigger and bigger issue," Bryan added.
Former Cleveland Fed President Lee Hoskins said the Fed must focus on the inflation trend rather than on its level.
After several years of declining CPI growth, the rate has recently begun to inch up toward 3.0 percent.
"The Fed needs to continue to watch the trend of inflation. The whole issue for the Fed is retaining credibility as an inflation fighter," said Hoskins, now chairman of Huntington National Bank.
"I would be more comfortable if the Fed would explicitly say what its targets are several years in advance," he added.
David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities, and a former St. Louis Fed economist, cautioned that the Boskin commission's findings do not guarantee the CPI will remain a reliable gauge.

"If we accept the Boskin commission finding that inflation has been overstated, we'll have no guarantee we won't have any distortion in the future," stressed Resler. "In a dynamic economy, we have constant changes in the product mix."
Resler said targeting CPI for monetary policy should imply targeting a range.
"You're never going to have a reliable measure of prices as a specific inflation target. But you can specify a range and that is something that should be reviewed annually," Resler concluded.
Bill Gavin, St. Louis Fed vice president for research, stressed there is a difference between the cost of living and using an inflation index level as target for monetary policy.
Gavin cited as an example the time when gold was a monetary policy anchor, with little impact on living costs.
"It's important to make a distinction between inflation as cost of living and a price index that should be stabilized by the monetary authority," Gavin said.
"It's not clear the Fed should necessarily be stabilizing the cost of living," he added.

"The idea we have a transparent goal for policy is very different from the cost of living. We are not at price stability yet," said Gavin, noting the Fed "looks at very many different measures of inflation" apart from the CPI.

The CPI bias issue has important bearings on efforts to balance the U.S. federal budget. A lower CPI would reduce spending on inflation-indexed government programs like Social Security. It would also boost tax revenues by reducing the annual inflation-adjusted increases in the standard deduction claimed by many taxpayers, as well as lowering the income level at which individuals enter higher tax brackets.
